title: The Question is Not What You Look At But What You See
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Prompted by a financial adviser friend whose colleagues repeatedly missed an obvious error in a report, Skelton distinguishes looking from noticing. Drawing on Thoreau, he defines noticing as isolating one specific thing from the general scene, and he links the colleagues' blindness to the stickiness and treading water that familiarity produces. He applies this to his own career: as a new teacher and later as a headteacher he looked at classrooms without seeing learning, and it took years to develop the detective's skill of isolating what matters. The argument is that Looking for Learning is really about noticing and seeing learning rather than general looking. He gives teachers and school leaders realistic, bounded ways to do this, such as carving out part of a lesson or part of a week for deliberate attention to learning.
points: Noticing is focused looking, a skill of isolating something specific from everything else in view, and it can be improved with practice.
Familiarity breeds comfortable blindness: repeated experience makes us look at everything and see nothing that matters.
Skelton admits he spent years in classrooms, as teacher and head, looking without seeing learning.
The remedy is modest and disciplined: set aside part of a lesson or week to attend only to whether learning is happening.
quotes: Noticing is focused looking. Noticing is isolating something from the generality of everything we are looking at and concentrating on something specific.

The majority of such reports his colleagues repeatedly look over are factually ok. They repeatedly use the same format. As we know, these repeated experiences breed stickiness and stickiness creates treading water.

The skill I wasn’t good at at all in my early days as a teacher (because I was at Beginning level) was the skill of the detective. I couldn’t scan my horizon, move on from the many things I was looking at and isolate something of importance, something that my mentor Fred reminded me was called learning.

I realise now that my visits to classrooms as a new Headteacher/Principal were often an opportunity to take a break and to refresh myself. Classrooms were places I deliberately went to so that I could generally look but not particularly see, where I coylds coast for a while.
We can’t isolate, notice and see learning all the time. We shouldn’t expect it of ourselves. But we do need to be disciplined enough to look for learning for some of the time, all of the time.

As Headteachers/Principals/school leaders, we can’t be in classes all of the time, and when we are in classrooms we won’t always have the time to notice and see learning. But we can carve out enough time in a week to visit classrooms and make a deliberate attempt to let most of our ordinary looking pass us by, isolate our thoughts around learning and then notice and see whether learning is happening (or not).
